data.question: Should we adopt sanction_lambda 0.5 → 0 (option 1), adopt block_k 3 → 2 over the 1-2 company vote (option 2), or keep v1 unchanged this period?
data.background: Option 1 removes all monetary enforcement of the road rules. It was put forward as the remedy for C that D1 and D2 required, so the human must decide whether removing sanctions, rather than redistributing them, is an acceptable remedy. Option 2 is the same block_k change that lost 1-2 votes in D1 and D2; adopting it now would be the first override of a two-of-three majority, which is a governance decision only the human can make. The two proposals were measured separately, not together, and should be read side by side.

options.summary: Sanctions for road-rule violations are removed (lambda 0.5 → 0). Every KPI measure gets worse. On-time falls from 213.6 to 204.0 (-9.6, 0/5 seeds improved), late rises from 9.2 to 18.8, p95_wait_s from 130 to 182, max_wait_s from 236 to 334, and the lowest on-time rate from 0.93 to 0.83. Blocked seconds rise from 1888 to 3085 and road violations from 24.2 to 44.6. Unfinished stays at 0.0. Votes: A ×, B ○, C ○, so it passes the rule-layer vote 2-1.
options.stakeholders: C gains the most (utility 58.3 → 70.2) and B gains slightly (69.6 → 71.0). A loses (70.2 → 62.8). Customers clearly lose: there are more late deliveries and much longer typical and worst-case waits. Road safety and order also suffer, because violations nearly double when they cost nothing.

options.summary: block_k drops from 3 to 2, adopted over the vote (A ○, B ×, C ×). On-time rises from 213.6 to 219.4 (+5.8, 3/5 seeds improved), late falls from 9.2 to 3.4, p95_wait_s from 130 to 93.2, max_wait_s from 236 to 224, and the lowest on-time rate rises from 0.93 to 0.96. Blocked seconds fall from 1888 to 1217, but road violations rise from 24.2 to 34.8. Unfinished stays at 0.0. This would be the first override of a majority vote.
options.stakeholders: Customers gain: fewer late deliveries and shorter waits. A gains (utility 70.2 → 75.6). B loses (69.6 → 62.5), and C loses heavily (58.3 → 46.9, -11.4). C was already the lowest-utility company. The companies' trust in the vote would be affected by a first override.

options.summary: Stay at v1 (block_k 3, lambda 0.5). Current values continue: on-time 213.6, late 9.2, p95_wait_s 130, max_wait_s 236, unfinished 0.0, road violations 24.2. Utility A / B / C stays 70.2 / 69.6 / 58.3.
options.stakeholders: The companies keep the status quo and the vote outcome is respected. Customers forgo the measured improvement from option 2, about 5.8 fewer on-time deliveries per run and a p95 wait of 130 s instead of 93.2 s. C stays the lowest-utility company with no remedy yet.

recommendation.reason: Option 1 is not an acceptable remedy for C. It worsens every KPI measure on all seeds (on-time -9.6, 0/5 seeds; p95_wait_s 130 → 182; max_wait_s 236 → 334) and nearly doubles road violations (24.2 → 44.6), so customers would pay for C's gain. Option 2 still lacks what D1 and D2 required: there is no remedy for C, and the table gives no per-company breakdown of the added road violations (24.2 → 34.8). Its gain is also weaker than before (+5.8 with 3/5 seeds, versus 5/5 seeds in D1 and D2), while C's loss is larger (-11.4). Overriding the majority on weaker evidence, with the D1 and D2 conditions unmet, would make those conditions meaningless. The next step should be a targeted remedy for C, for example a partial lambda reduction or a redistribution of the sanctions, measured together with block_k=2 and with a per-company violation breakdown.
assumptions: The current-period measurements reflect the coming period's demand.
Removing lambda fully is the only sanction variant that was measured; partial reductions or redistributions might behave differently.
Option 2's re-measurement did not produce the per-company violation breakdown, because the table does not show one.
The companies' votes reflect stable preferences that a better-designed remedy could change.

unknowns: The per-company, per-type and per-severity breakdown of the added road violations under block_k=2, and whether the Major eviction sanctions mostly fall on C.
The combined effect of block_k=2 with a reduced or redistributed sanction (lambda 0, or a value between 0 and 0.5), which was not measured.
Whether C or B would vote for block_k=2 if a targeted remedy accompanied it.
Each company's behavioural policy: whether violations would keep rising over time if sanctions were removed.
How customers perceive the longer waits under option 1 or the remaining late deliveries under keep.
Next period's demand level, and whether option 2's gain (3/5 seeds) is robust in busier or quieter periods.
The long-term effect on the companies' trust in governance of a first override of a majority vote.
